title: Puto
intro: Small, fluffy steamed rice cakes, lightly sweet with a soft coconut flavor. They are eaten on their own for merienda or alongside dinuguan.

items.name: butter
items.note: melted, plus more for the molds

steps.text: Bring water to a boil in a steamer. Brush the puto molds (about 2 inches across) with melted butter or oil.
Whisk the rice flour, sugar, baking powder and salt in a bowl.
Add the coconut milk, water and melted butter and whisk until smooth, with no lumps, like a thick pancake batter. Let it rest so the flour hydrates.
Fill the molds three-quarters full. Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes.
Steam over medium-high heat until the cakes have risen, split slightly on top and a toothpick comes out clean.
Let the puto cool in the molds, then loosen the edges with a small spatula and unmold. Steam the rest of the batter the same way.

tips: Do not open the lid during the first 10 minutes or the cakes can sink. Puto keeps 2 days covered at room temperature or 5 days in the fridge; re-steam for 3 minutes to soften.

title: Cheese puto
intro: Soft, sweet steamed cakes made with flour and milk, each crowned with a strip of cheese that softens on top. A favorite for parties and school snacks.

items.name: butter
items.note: melted, plus more for the molds

steps.text: Bring water to a boil in a steamer. Brush the puto molds (about 2 inches across) with melted butter or oil.
Sift the flour, sugar, baking powder and salt into a bowl.
In another bowl beat the egg with the evaporated milk, water and melted butter. Pour into the dry ingredients and whisk just until smooth.
Fill the molds three-quarters full. Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes. Steam over medium-high heat until risen and set.
Lay a strip of cheese on each cake and steam until the cheese softens and a toothpick comes out clean.
Cool the puto in the molds, then unmold. Steam the rest of the batter the same way.

tips: Quick-melt cheese gives the classic soft topping; cheddar stays firmer and saltier. Sifting keeps the crumb fine and even.

title: Ube puto
intro: Purple steamed rice cakes made with ube halaya, so they taste of real purple yam with a mild coconut sweetness. Soft and slightly dense, they hold up well for packing.

items.name: butter
items.note: melted, plus more for the molds

steps.text: Bring water to a boil in a steamer. Brush the puto molds (about 2 inches across) with melted butter or oil.
Whisk the ube halaya with the coconut milk, water, melted butter and ube extract until no lumps of halaya remain.
Whisk the rice flour, sugar, baking powder and salt in a large bowl. Pour in the ube mixture and whisk to a smooth batter. Let it rest.
Fill the molds three-quarters full. Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes.
Steam over medium-high heat until risen and a toothpick comes out clean.
Cool the puto in the molds, then unmold. Steam the rest of the batter the same way.

tips: Store-bought ube halaya varies in sweetness: taste the batter and add a spoonful more sugar if yours is mild.

title: Pandan puto
intro: Pale green steamed rice cakes flavored with fresh pandan juice, fragrant and lightly sweet. They are served with freshly grated coconut on top.

items.name: pandan leaves
items.note: fresh or frozen, cut into pieces

steps.text: Blend the pandan leaves with the water until finely chopped, then squeeze through a fine sieve or cloth. You need 3/4 cup green juice; top up with water if short.
Bring water to a boil in a steamer. Brush the puto molds (about 2 inches across) with melted butter or oil.
Whisk the rice flour, sugar, baking powder and salt. Add the pandan juice, coconut milk and oil and whisk until smooth. Let the batter rest.
Fill the molds three-quarters full. Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes. Steam over medium-high heat until risen and a toothpick comes out clean.
Cool in the molds, then unmold and top each cake with grated coconut.

tips: Fresh pandan gives a soft natural green. A drop of pandan paste brightens the color, but the flavor comes from the leaves. Eat coconut-topped puto the same day.

title: Chocolate puto
intro: Cocoa-flavored steamed cakes with a soft, springy crumb, somewhere between puto and a chocolate cupcake. Kids like them plain or with a little cheese on top.

items.name: butter
items.note: melted, plus more for the molds

steps.text: Bring water to a boil in a steamer. Brush the puto molds (about 2 inches across) with melted butter or oil.
Sift the flour, cocoa, sugar, baking powder and salt together into a bowl.
Beat the egg with the milk and melted butter, pour into the dry ingredients and whisk just until smooth.
Fill the molds three-quarters full. Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes. Steam over medium-high heat until risen and a toothpick comes out clean.
Cool the puto in the molds, then unmold. Steam the rest of the batter the same way.

tips: Sift the cocoa: lumps stay as dry pockets in the cakes. For a sweet and salty finish, lay a sliver of cheese on top for the last 2 minutes of steaming.

title: Puto Manapla
intro: Large rice cakes steamed in banana-leaf-lined molds from freshly ground soaked rice. They are firmer and a little coarser than flour puto, lightly sweet, with the scent of the leaf.

items.name: banana leaves
items.note: wilted over a flame, for lining

steps.text: Drain the soaked rice. Blend it with the water in a high-speed blender until completely smooth, about 3 minutes; a drop rubbed between your fingers should not feel gritty.
Pour the batter into a bowl and whisk in the sugar and salt until dissolved.
Line four 5-inch round molds (llaneras or small cake pans) with banana leaves and bring the steamer to a boil. Whisk the baking powder into the batter.

Pour the batter into the molds about three-quarters full. Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes. Steam over medium-high heat until risen, firm and a toothpick comes out clean.
Cool the cakes in the molds, then unmold, peel off the leaves if you like and cut into wedges.

tips: Soak the rice at least 8 hours or overnight before blending. If the batter still feels gritty, let it rest 30 minutes and blend again.

title: Puto Calasiao
intro: Bite-size, chewy rice cakes made from a lightly fermented rice batter, so they taste sweet with a faint tang. Snow white and springy, they are eaten by the handful.

steps.text: Drain the rice and blend with the water until very smooth, about 3 minutes.
Whisk in the sugar, salt and yeast. Cover and leave in a warm spot until the batter is bubbly and smells slightly sour, 4 to 6 hours.
Stir the batter down and whisk in the baking powder. Oil tiny molds (about 1 1/2 inches across) and bring the steamer to a boil.
Fill the molds almost to the top. Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes. Steam over high heat until puffed and set.
Cool briefly, then pop the cakes out of the molds. Steam the rest of the batter the same way.

tips: Plan ahead: the rice soaks overnight and the batter needs 4 to 6 hours to ferment. If it smells strongly sour, whisk in a spoonful more sugar before steaming.

title: Puto Biñan
intro: A round steamed rice cake set in a banana-leaf-lined pan and topped with salted egg and grated cheese. Soft and buttery, sweet and salty at once.

steps.text: Line an 8-inch round pan with banana leaves and bring the steamer to a boil.
Whisk the rice flour, sugar, baking powder and salt. Beat the eggs with the coconut milk, water and melted butter, then whisk into the dry ingredients until smooth.
Pour the batter into the pan. Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes. Steam over medium-high heat until the top is set.
Arrange the salted egg slices and cheese on top and steam until a toothpick comes out clean.
Brush the warm cake with softened butter, let it cool a little, then cut into wedges.

tips: Add the toppings only once the surface has set, or they sink into the batter.

title: Puto pao
intro: Soft steamed puto with a pocket of sweet and savory pork asado in the middle, like a small siopao made with puto batter. A filling merienda that travels well.

items.name: butter
items.note: melted, plus more for the molds

steps.text: Heat the oil in a small pan and saute the garlic and onion until soft. Add the pork and cook until no longer pink.
Add the soy sauce, brown sugar and water. Cover and simmer until the pork is tender and most of the liquid has reduced.
Stir in the cornstarch mixture and cook until the filling is thick and glossy. Let it cool completely.
Bring water to a boil in a steamer and butter 18 puto molds.
Sift the flour, sugar, baking powder and salt. Beat the egg with the evaporated milk, water and melted butter and whisk into the dry ingredients until smooth.
Spoon batter into each mold one-third full, add 1 heaping tsp of filling, then cover with batter to three-quarters full. Top with a strip of cheese if using.
Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes. Steam over medium-high heat until risen and a toothpick inserted beside the filling comes out clean.
Cool the puto in the molds, then unmold.

tips: Make the filling a day ahead and chill it: cold, thick filling stays in the center instead of sinking.

title: Puto flan
intro: Two-layer steamed cakes with a smooth leche flan on top and soft, fluffy puto underneath. Rich, eggy and sweet, they are a step up from plain puto for parties.

items.name: butter
items.note: melted, plus more for the molds

steps.text: Butter 16 puto molds generously and bring the steamer to a gentle simmer.
Gently whisk the egg yolks, condensed milk, evaporated milk and vanilla without making froth, then strain. Pour about 1 tbsp into each mold.
Steam over low heat with the lid slightly ajar until the flan is just set.
Meanwhile whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder and salt. Beat the egg with the evaporated milk and melted butter and whisk into the flour until smooth.

Spoon the batter over the set flan to three-quarters full. Raise the heat to medium-high. Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes. Steam until the puto is puffed and a toothpick comes out clean.
Cool, loosen the edges with a thin knife and turn the cakes out flan side up.

tips: Steam the flan on low heat; high heat makes it bubbly and full of holes. The same cakes are also sold as leche puto.

title: Puto lanson
intro: Steamed grated cassava sweetened with sugar and coconut, cut into squares and topped with more fresh coconut. Chewy and moist, with a clean cassava flavor.

items.name: cassava
items.note: peeled and finely grated, or frozen grated cassava, thawed

steps.text: Squeeze the grated cassava in a cloth to remove excess liquid; it should be moist but not dripping.
Mix the cassava with the sugar, salt and 1 cup grated coconut.
Line an 8-inch square pan with banana leaves, brush with coconut oil and press the mixture in evenly.
Steam over medium-high heat until the whole cake is translucent and firm.
Cool at least 20 minutes for clean cuts, then slice into squares and top with grated coconut.

tips: Raw cassava looks white and opaque: steam longer if any spots remain. Leftovers keep 2 days in the fridge; steam briefly to soften.

title: Puto maya
intro: Sticky glutinous rice steamed with coconut milk and ginger, packed into rounds and served warm. Often paired with ripe mango and thick hot chocolate in the morning.

items.name: banana leaves
items.note: or cheesecloth, for lining the steamer

steps.text: Drain the rice. Line a steamer basket with banana leaf or cheesecloth, spread the rice on it and steam until tender but still a little firm.
Warm the coconut milk with the sugar, salt and ginger until the sugar dissolves.
Turn the rice into a bowl, pour in the coconut milk and mix well. Let it absorb.
Return the rice to the lined steamer and steam until glossy, sticky and fully tender.
Remove the ginger slices. Pack the rice into small cups or a ramekin and unmold onto plates. Serve warm with mango.

tips: Soaking matters: unsoaked rice stays hard in the center. Leftovers firm up in the fridge; re-steam for 5 minutes.

title: Puto kutsinta
intro: Two favorites in one bite: a chewy brown kutsinta base under a fluffy white puto top. Sweet, soft and bouncy, with a little cheese on top if you like.

items.name: butter
items.note: melted, plus more for the molds

steps.text: Dissolve the brown sugar and annatto powder in the water. Whisk in the flour and tapioca starch until smooth, then stir in the lye water. Let it rest.
Butter 18 puto molds and bring the steamer to a boil. Stir the kutsinta batter and fill each mold one-third full. Steam until set and no longer sticky to the touch.
Meanwhile whisk the flour, sugar and baking powder. Beat the egg with the evaporated milk, water and butter and whisk into the flour until smooth.
Spoon the puto batter over the set kutsinta to three-quarters full and top with cheese. Steam until puffed and a toothpick comes out clean from the top layer.
Cool completely so the kutsinta firms, then unmold.

tips: Lye water is strong: measure it level and keep it away from children. The kutsinta layer must be set before the puto batter goes on or the layers blur.

title: Kutsinta
intro: Bouncy, jelly-like steamed cakes made with brown sugar and lye water, with a deep caramel flavor. They are served with freshly grated coconut on top.

steps.text: Dissolve the brown sugar and annatto powder in the water; warm water helps. Let it cool.
Whisk the flour and tapioca starch into the syrup until smooth, strain, then stir in the lye water. Let the batter rest.
Oil the molds and bring the steamer to a boil. Stir the batter, since the starch settles, and fill the molds nearly full.
Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes. Steam over medium heat until the cakes are set, translucent and springy.
Cool completely before unmolding; kutsinta firms up as it cools.
Serve topped with grated coconut.

tips: Too much lye water makes kutsinta bitter, too little leaves it soft and sticky. Stir the batter before filling each round of molds.

title: Ube kutsinta
intro: Purple kutsinta flavored with ube, with the same bouncy, chewy bite as the brown classic but a milder, sweeter taste. Topped with grated coconut or cheese.

steps.text: Dissolve the sugar in the water, then whisk in the ube halaya and ube extract until smooth.
Whisk in the flour and tapioca starch, strain, then stir in the lye water. Let the batter rest.
Oil the molds and bring the steamer to a boil. Stir the batter and fill the molds nearly full.
Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes. Steam over medium heat until set and springy.
Cool completely before unmolding.
Serve topped with grated coconut or cheese.

tips: Strain the batter after adding the halaya so no lumps reach the molds. White sugar keeps the purple bright; brown sugar turns it muddy.

title: Pandan kutsinta
intro: Green kutsinta made with fresh pandan juice, bouncy and chewy with a sweet, grassy fragrance. Served with plenty of grated coconut.

steps.text: Blend the pandan leaves with the water until finely chopped, then squeeze through a cloth. Top up with water to 2 1/2 cups.
Dissolve the sugar in the pandan juice. Whisk in the flour and tapioca starch, strain, then stir in the lye water. Let it rest.
Oil the molds and bring the steamer to a boil. Stir the batter and fill the molds nearly full.
Wrap the steamer lid in a kitchen towel so condensation does not drip onto the cakes. Steam over medium heat until set and springy.
Cool completely before unmolding.
Serve topped with grated coconut.

tips: Mature, dark leaves give the strongest color and aroma. A drop of pandan paste brightens the green without changing the method.

title: Sapin-sapin
intro: Layered sticky rice cake in purple, yellow and white, each layer flavored differently: ube, jackfruit and plain coconut. Soft, chewy and sweet, finished with crunchy latik.

steps.text: Whisk all the base batter ingredients until smooth. Divide into three equal portions, about 1 1/2 cups each.
Whisk the ube halaya and ube extract into one portion and the jackfruit and food coloring into the second. Leave the third plain.
Grease an 8-inch square pan with coconut oil and bring the steamer to a boil. Pour in the ube layer, cover with a towel-wrapped lid and steam until set.
Pour the jackfruit layer over the set ube layer and steam until set.
Pour the plain layer on top and steam until the whole cake is firm and translucent.
Cool completely, at least 1 hour, then slice with an oiled knife and top with latik.

tips: Add each layer only after the one below has set, or the colors run together. An oiled knife or a length of thread gives the cleanest cuts.

title: Puto bumbong
intro: Purple sticky rice logs steamed until tender, then spread with butter and showered with muscovado and grated coconut. This home version uses a regular steamer and banana leaves instead of bamboo tubes.

steps.text: Mix the flours and salt. Stir the ube extract into the water, then drizzle it over the flour while rubbing with your fingertips until the mix looks like damp sand and holds together when squeezed but crumbles easily. Do not knead it into a dough.
Press the mixture through a coarse sieve to break up lumps and keep it light.
Brush the banana leaves with butter. Spoon about 1/4 cup of the crumbs in a line along each leaf, roll the leaf loosely around it into a log and fold the ends. Do not pack it.
Steam over high heat until the logs are purple, translucent and cooked through. Steam in batches if needed.
Unwrap onto a plate while hot, spread with butter and sprinkle with muscovado and grated coconut.

tips: If you have bamboo tubes or a puto bumbong steamer, fill the tubes loosely with the same crumbs and steam 8 to 10 minutes. The texture depends on keeping the mix crumbly, not wet.

title: Kapampangan tamales
intro: Rice flour and coconut milk cooked into a thick, nutty paste, then wrapped in banana leaves with chicken, salted egg and peanuts and steamed. Savory with a gentle sweetness, for merienda or breakfast.

steps.text: Heat the oil with the annatto seeds over low heat until the oil turns deep orange, about 3 minutes. Strain and discard the seeds.
In a heavy pot, whisk the rice flour into the coconut milk until smooth. Add the ground peanuts, sugar, salt and pepper.
Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until it becomes a thick paste that pulls away from the sides of the pot.
Move one-third of the mixture to a bowl and stir in the annatto oil until evenly orange.

Lay two leaves on top of each other. Spread 1/3 cup of the white mixture into a rectangle, top with 1 tbsp of the orange mixture, some chicken, a wedge of salted egg and a few peanuts. Fold into a packet and tie.
Steam the packets until heated through and firm.
Serve warm in the leaves.

tips: Two layers of leaf keep steam from seeping in; foil around each packet works too. Tamales keep 3 days in the fridge; re-steam for 10 minutes.

title: Pintos
intro: Freshly grated young corn mixed with milk, butter and sugar, wrapped in its own husks and steamed into soft, sweet little cakes. They taste like the sweetest part of the corn.

steps.text: Peel the husks carefully, keeping the large inner ones whole, and rinse them. Cut the kernels off the cobs; you need about 4 cups.
Blend the kernels with the milk to a thick, slightly coarse puree.
Stir in the sugar, melted butter, salt and cheese if using.
Overlap two husks, spoon about 1/3 cup of the mixture into the center, fold in the sides and then the ends, and tie with a thin strip of husk.
Lay the packets seam side down in the steamer and steam until firm when pressed.
Let them rest before unwrapping so they set.

tips: Use young, milky corn: older, starchy kernels make dry pintos. If the husks tear, wrap the packets in foil.
